Messages.Author: Madman2001
Messages.Body:
Folks:

Does the initial life total for an ally constitute a ceiling for that
ally's life total?

For example, the Succubus can steal a blood or life to gain 1 life.
Although the Succubus starts with 3 life, I can find no rule that would
prevent the Succubus from walking around with, say, 10 life if she
could successfully perform her built-in action 7 times.

From discussions on this newsgroup, I find that most folks are negative
about the allies. Is it because allies cannot generally use combat or
action cards??

Anyway, as always, thanks for your insights,
Madman

Messages.Author: Steve Wampler
Messages.Body:
Madman2001 wrote:
<snip>

> From discussions on this newsgroup, I find that most folks are negative
> about the allies. Is it because allies cannot generally use combat or
> action cards??

This sounds like a fun thread : )

Anyway, the reasons that allies suck can be divided into 3 basic
categories:
1) Cost
2) Uselessness
3) Fragileness

-COST-
The pool cost for most allies is in the same ball park as small
vampires, so from that perspective the cost is not unreasonable.
However, the opportunity costs are very very high. Recruiting an ally
costs an action from a vampire. That means one less bleed, vote, rush
or other action. In many cases the vampire must also be of a specific
clan in order to recruit the ally, which makes mixing and matching
allies much more difficult than doing the same for vampires. The ally
card also takes up space in your library instead of your crpyt, where
space is more precious. This is also important because many allies are
unique, so you must find that balance between including enough so that
you get one, but not so many that they jam your hand.

-USELESSNESS-
Sure, an ally probably costs you a bit less than a vampire, but what are
you gonna do with it? Some allies do have useful special abilities, but
most lack fundamental abilities of vampires, especially bleeding and the
ability to call votes.
Allies also lack disciplines, which are what the game revolves around.

-FRAGILENESS-
Allies are even more overcosted when one considers their great
propensity for getting killed. In general, they have fewer life points
than their cost, whereas vampires have "life" equal to their capacity
which is also their cost. Also note that vampires survive with no blood
whereas allies die when they have 0 life. Allies also cannot hunt to
regain life and do not have a "torpor" state- they are burned, which
makes them much *much* harder to recover than torporized vampires.

Overall, allies are far to costly for the limited benefits they
provide. There are, of course, a few exceptions. Renegade Garou are
popular because of their terrifying combat abilities and Arms Dealers
are good because of their low cost.

--
Steve Wampler

>However, the opportunity costs are very very high. Recruiting an ally
>costs an action from a vampire. That means one less bleed, vote, rush

I don't think the action argument holds water. It may cost an action
but it doesn't cost any transfers, which is another scarce resource you
need to bring out vampires. If you've got lots of weeny vampires already
out and one or more of them don't really have anything else you want
done (too full to hunt, bleed would only get them trashed at the moment,
leaving them untapped for later not necessary, etc. etc.) then an action
spent to recruit an ally may be completely painless. OTOH, I've noticed
that one sort-of major problem with weeny decks is how you can get bolluxed
up spending transfers to bring up vampires and then bringing them into
the active region.

In general though, it's kind of pointless comparing an action to a
number of tranfers. When looking at allies, the real question is, "Is
this thing worth its overall cost, including the action it takes to recruit,
in this deck?" And in making this comparison, of course, you take into
account the other stuff you talked about: uselessness (in many cases) and
fragileness (is that really a word? :) ). I do agree with your eventual
conclusion: most allies just aren't worth their cost. I don't know what it
is but for whatever reasons, the designers just seemed to habitually
overestimate the value of allies when setting their pool costs. (Let alone
a number of various silly cards intended to "hose" allies which got printed
and never see much play because few games are ever overrun with allies.)

Fred

Hey, if it's worth anything, I LOVE allies! I'll be the first to admit that
most of them suck, but it's sort of fun and amusing. In fact, in my current
deck (which I got some great feedback here, and which I'll post a revised
edition and ask for more help later), I have four or five allies.

Yes, they can be a bit expensive, but as Fred mentioned, they don't cost
transfers. Interestingly enough, I tried to make the same point (that allies
would speed up a deck), but the general consensus is that it actually slows the
deck down.

I personally use Mage allies (for my Tremere theme deck), and while they are
among the more expensive allies, at least they have some semi-decent combat
ability. Of course they'll get cremated by combat decks, but at least they do
SOME damage and against non-combat decks, a manuever and ranged damage is
pretty good. Yes, most allies can't use disciplines (though a few can. Ghouled
Street something has basic Potence, and Talaq the Immortal has basic Quietus
and Thaumaturgy), so I sometimes include a few Dodges or Fake Outs, which can
also be used by my small vampires in a jam.

There is no limit to an ally's life counters. Generally this isn't a problem.
VERY few allies are able to increase their life. Renegade Garou, Hell Hound,
and Black Spiral Buddy regenerate, but they only regenerate to their normal
max. Gargoyle Slave has a "retarded" version of regeneration (they have to
take an action to get the life back), but is otherwise like the above. Off the
top of my head, only Succubus (with her stealing action), Nephandus (with her
"diablerie"-like action), and Talaq (with lots of Thefts of Vitae) can gain
lots of life. And though an ally with 100 life may seem formidable, as said
earlier, allies are VERY vulnerable. There are many cards that burn allies
outright (Kindred Segregation, Blood to Water, one of the Obtenebration cards,
etc.), and they are notoriously vulnerable to other "control" cards (Art of
Love, Far Mastery, Entrancement, etc.).

Oh, quick question. For corruption counter junk, do you use the ally's current
life points, or initial amount? Or it's the latter, the 100 point ally can be
corrupted after only a few corruption counters!

I personally don't really like how WotC handled allies in this game. Ghouls
and normal mortals are decent, but mages and werewolves should at least be
comparable to vampires. But then again, this IS a game ABOUT vampires...

Halcyan 2

You do realize your argument sums up as: if your deck is completely
stalled, and your minions have nothing to do, allies might be
usefull?

In general, in my experience, actions are definitely more important
than transfers. Transfers tend to cost you pool. You need some,
but more isn't in general neccesarily better. In particular,
once you can't afford any more transfers, they're worthless.

If you could bring allies in with transfers rather than actions,
they'd still suck. Not as much though, which is a good indication
that actions are indeed more expensive.

Have wondered about the poor cost effectiveness of allies for a long
time until I ran across an article about "Concealed Weapon." Where
"Concealed Weapon" is identified as a Disciplineless card rather than
an Obfuscate card. Quick reference to both "Concealed Weapon" and it's
cousin "Disguised Weapon" show them to be close in operation with
"Concealed Weapon" being the weaker of the two. "Concealed Weapon" has
no Basic or Superior text like "Disguised Weapon" and is limited the
types of weapons that can be brought to bear.

"Concealed Weapon" with allies just seem to go hand in hand. It gives
them greater latitude and increases their potential as a usable minion
and the use of "Concealed Weapon" could also be applied to vampires as
well.

I have once before inquired if anyone has playtested "Concealed Weapon"
as a disciplineless card and never received an answer. Whether this is
because no has done it (unlikely as I have come across decks that
identify themselves as doing so) or there has already been a "Flame
War" over this subject and I missed it.

The only arguments I have heard on this subject were:
"the card is from the Jyhad set and not readily available to
everyone" (which I think is rubbish... prior to coming out to Germany
I was able to purchase 10 boxes of boosters for $100 and that was less
than a year ago)
"some allies (i.e. Hell Hound) do not have the ability to use
weapons and "Concealed Weapon" gives a loop hole to equiping with a
weapon" (this argument is the strongest one of the two and 'yes' I do
agree with this particular argument)

Despite the second argument, I personally feel that "Concealed Weapon"
as a disciplineless card does have merit. I have not playtested the
concept with my group but believe it would give more life to the use of
"Weapons" and "Allies" within the game.

Just my 2 cents...

Mike Eichler
(Prince of Ramstein)

Sent via Deja.com http://www.deja.com/
Before you buy.

In Austin, we have played with Concealed Weapon as a disciplineless
card for many years now. In most decks, guns are overcosted, and
having that extra card in hand when you don't have any guns is pretty
useless. Occasionally, someone will pull out a deck with CW and guns,
but never so far with Allies and CW and guns.

This would be too many combinations of fragile items.
Your ally maneuvers to long with his .44, Sarah Cobbler steals
his 2 life with Theft of Vitae, both the gun and the ally go poof!

Eight of the fourteen Sabbat allies are killed by Theft of Vitae.
Seventeen of the twenty-four other allies are killed by Theft of Vitae.
Nine allies are killed by Catatonic Fear at superior. Twenty-five
allies are killed by Riposte at superior. All allies are killed by
Entombment at close range. All allies (except Ambrosius) are killed by
Immortal Grapple/(SUP)Torn Signpost/(SUP)Pushing the Limit.

Even with CW to get the gun on the Ally without an action,
combining the two together is a mistake in almost every case.

The only allies that I would bother to give a weapon are War Ghouls and
Ambrosius, the Ferryman (Wraith). War Ghoul's with Stakes have been
known to sweep tables. http://members.tripod.com/~Lasombra/wgfinal.htm
But even in that deck, the card cost/opportunity cost of concealed
weapon is way too high. I use Vast Wealth cards instead.
Ambrosius with Talbot's Chainsaw is great too, but watch out for
those damn Tremere. http://members.tripod.com/~Lasombra/Ambrosius.htm

Guns cost too much and are too fragile, you may never reap
any damage from them before you vampire/ally is destroyed.
Concealed Weapon does not help enough to make any real difference
and does not get played with either Vampires or Allies.

Carpe Noctem.

Lasombra

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Mike Eichler wrote:
>>I have once before inquired if anyone has playtested "Concealed Weapon"
as a disciplineless card and never received an answer. Whether this is
because no has done it (unlikely as I have come across decks that
identify themselves as doing so) or there has already been a "Flame
War" over this subject and I missed it.>>

Plently of people have played with this house rule over the years, and it has
been debated extensively in this forum (check out deja-news if you wanna find
the old posts). While most people agree that it was probably, at one point in
production, meant to be disciplineless, it was changed to require Obfuscate.
This might have been a complete accident/misprint; or it might have been due to
someone at the last minute deciding that if it were disciplinless it would have
been too useful (although I find this somewhat unlikely--it is far more likely
to be due to someone screwing something up).

Regardless of the reason Concealed Weapon became an Obfuscate card, one of the
main precepts of errating cards is to only downgrade cards that are too good,
not to upgrade cards that are too weak (that, and repair recognized misprints,
and CW has never been positively identified as a misprint). Cards that are too
good have a negative impact upon the game environment, while cards that are too
weak have no effect upon play, as they simply get ignored. If you are going to
fix CW, you are then going to have to fix Chainsaw, Werewolf Pack, Mercy of the
Weak, and countless other weak cards. Not a can of worms that is worth opening.

This being said, I can't really see how making CW disciplinless would really
make allies any more useful. All it would mean is that when your Thadeous Zho
gets a magnum without wasting an action, he will cost you 6 pool when he dies,
instead of just 4. Guns aren't that good. Allies aren't that good. Combine
them, and you have extra not good.

The only allies that I have ever seen useful have been:

Renegade Garou/Muddles: Very useful against weenie or low combat defense decks,
but often just get killed in one shot, costing you a great deal of pool (well,
for Garou anyways).

Arms Dealer: Very effective, 'cause he is free. Build a deck with cheap brujah
and 20 or so Arms Dealers. You can make an army of disposable minions for
nothing--send them computer hacking or buying guns or whatever. Not a truly
effective deck, but Arms Dealer is the best bargain you are going to get in an
ally.

Political Ally: Occasionally effective in the right deck--he is cheap and has a
built in bleed of three. You just leave him around as a threat and bleed with
other minions. If your prey has to chose between a bleed of 1 from a vampire or
a known bleed of 3 from the Politico, your 1 point bleed is going to get
through, at which point you jack it up. Not really effective, but can be
useful.

>>Despite the second argument, I personally feel that "Concealed Weapon"
as a disciplineless card does have merit. I have not playtested the
concept with my group but believe it would give more life to the use of
"Weapons" and "Allies" within the game.>>

It clearly has merit, but I suspect it does not have enough merit to justify
setting an errata precident (that the rules team is willing to errata weak
cards just to make them more useful), and I still don't think it will help
allies much, if at all.

LSJ and every Rules Team before him, has acknowledged that Concealed
Weapon was probably a misprint for many reasons. Every Rules Team
has also said that they would not errata cards to make them more
powerful. The purpose of errata is to bring the cost of cards in
line with similar cards, or to correct game breaking mistakes.

Keeping CW as an obfuscate card does not make it overpowered.

In other words, it does not break or hurt the game to leave it
as it is. It will not be changed at a national level unless
it gets reprinted, and we can all hope that WOTC has better ideas
for cards to print than that.

This whole argument is one of the reasons it was not reprinted
when it the backs changed to VTES.

Go back over the arguments some time at Mark Langdorf's site:

http://www.io.com/~mlangsdo/RPGs/Jyhad/

And look in the section on Broken Cards.

Messages.Author: R. David Zopf
Messages.Body:
Madman2001 wrote in message ...

>Folks:
>
>Does the initial life total for an ally constitute a ceiling for that
>ally's life total?
>

Nope.

>From discussions on this newsgroup, I find that most folks are negative
>about the allies. Is it because allies cannot generally use combat or
>action cards??
>

Most people just haven't tried to make allies the focus of thier strategy.
I've two decks at the Lasombra's fine archive
(members.tripod.com/`Lasombra/rdz.htm) that make use of allies to a
relatively high level of effect. 21 Burst Salute uses Talaq the Immortal
and Shadow Court Satyr along with a multitude of Busrt of Sunlight.
Make Allies Cheap uses Arms Dealers sacrificed for War Ghouls, along
with the classic "Ambrosius, the Ferryman equipped with Talbot's Chainsaw"
combo.
Both of these can benefit from Nephandus as torpor cleanup, since
burning vamps with allies rarely happens.
Both also have some common tactics that make the investment in allies
worthwhile. First, the use of Compel the Spirit (either wiht nec skill
cards, or a few copies of Rudolpho Giovanni in the crypt). Second, the use
of small vamires in recruiting (and blood gain for them when they aren't
recruiting allies). Finally, the use of disciplineless combat cards.
You've got to be _very_ aware of who you're target is with this sort of
combat, and avoid those who might do you harm. Fortunately, these decks can
be easily changed to weenie light bleed mid-game if you are at some point
stonewalled by an ally combat-ready prey.
By no means would I consider Allies a tournament ready tactic. But they
do have a certain surprise element that other deck ideas lack, that's their
best advantage.

Regards,
R. David Zopf
Atom Weaver
V:EKN Prince of Charlotte, NC

I'm not sure where you read that. All I said was that if *one* minion
you have doesn't have another productive action to take and you don't
feel you gain much (or anything) by leaving it untapped, tapping it to
recruit is a negligible cost. That's hardly the same thing as my deck
being completely stalled out. If you can't imagine any other distinctions
between the two, at least consider that I'm good to go for many bleeds next
turn but in the process of setting myself up for it, it's pointless to do
it this turn because I don't have more potential bleeders than my prey has
interceptors. So wait until next turn when all my minions are untapped (or
I'm ready to pay for Misdirection or whatever), and in the mean time, tap
that doing-nothing weeny to recruit an ally and exercise my hand to boot.
Now, does that sound like the same thing as being completely stalled?

>than transfers. Transfers tend to cost you pool. You need some,
>but more isn't in general neccesarily better. In particular,
>once you can't afford any more transfers, they're worthless.

In general, you may be right. But that may not be true for certain decks,
in which case, you need to calculate the cost of the action vs. the
transfers differently. That's all I'm saying.

>If you could bring allies in with transfers rather than actions,
>they'd still suck.

Unforunately, I have to agree with that one, at least for most allies.
Kind of sad - the game would definitely be much richer if the designers
had set the pool costs of the allies better (that is, smaller for most
of them).

Fred
